title: Dynamics of Flat-Top--Bubble Vector Solitons
authors: M. O. D. Alotaibi, L. Al Sakkaf, U. Al Khawaja
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of two-component flat-top--bubble vector solitons using a variational approximation and numerical simulations. The system is described by coupled cubic-quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equations with repulsive intercomponent coupling. We introduce a self-induced mechanism in which a localized flat-top soliton (FTS) generates a density bubble in a second component: the localized density acts as a repulsive potential for the background field, creating a composite bound state. A background-subtracted formulation and normalized super-Gaussian profiles yield collective-coordinate equations for the component centers and an effective interaction potential for their relative separation. The potential forms a binding well that is nearly triangular over its global displacement range but smooth and locally parabolic near its minimum. The variational approximation consequently predicts harmonic internal oscillations whose frequency is independent of amplitude in the small-oscillation regime. Real-time simulations verify this weak-kick behavior with good agreement between the variational and numerical frequencies. For strong phase imprints, equating the exact kick energy to the variational binding depth predicts a kick scale \(K_{\mathrm{escape}}\) for the onset of partial FTS escape. Real-time simulations support this prediction: below this scale, the composite remains nearly intact, whereas above it, a substantial fraction of the localized component leaves the bubble.
summary: This work analyzes the dynamics of two-component vector solitons governed by nonlinear Schrödinger equations. By employing a variational approach, the authors predict the internal oscillation frequency and establish a critical energy threshold for soliton stability. Simulations confirm that above this threshold, the localized component can partially escape the background density bubble.
main_problem: The paper investigates the dynamics of two-component flat-top--bubble vector solitons, focusing on their internal oscillations and the conditions for partial escape.
main_result: The system exhibits weak internal oscillations whose frequency is predicted to be independent of amplitude, and a critical energy scale ($K_{	ext{escape}}$) was determined above which the localized component substantially escapes the background bubble.
method: The dynamics are analyzed using a variational approximation applied to a background-subtracted formulation, supplemented by real-time numerical simulations.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by coupled cubic-quintic nonlinear Schrödinger equations describing two interacting components: a localized flat-top soliton (FTS) and a background density bubble. The interaction forms a composite bound state.
key_observables: Internal mode frequency ($\omega$), relative separation ($\ell(t)$), and the fraction of the FTS norm remaining within the bubble ($F_{	ext{bubble}}(t)$).
important_parameters: The escape energy scale ($K_{	ext{escape}}$) and the coupling/nonlinearity parameters ($g, q, ho_0$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on using normalized super-Gaussian profiles (ansatz) for the collective coordinates and assumes the background is modulationally stable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the variational binding potential, time evolution of component densities for coupled vs. decoupled states, and the dependence of oscillation frequency and component integrity on the strength of an external phase kick.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the model, developing the variational approximation using super-Gaussian ansatz, presenting numerical verification of internal oscillations, and finally using energy matching to predict the critical escape scale.
why_interesting: The study of soliton dynamics, particularly the interplay between localized structures (FTS) and background fields (bubble), is highly relevant to nonlinear wave physics, which shares mathematical techniques with Bose-Einstein Condensates (BECs) and nonlinear optics.
